title: What is a PIVOT operation (turn row values into columns, e.g. average salary per job title across departments), and how do you achieve the same portably with conditional aggregation (`SUM(CASE WHEN ... END)`) when the engine has no `PIVOT` keyword?
topicTitle: Aggregation — GROUP BY, HAVING, COUNT, SUM

s1_definition.profdef: A PIVOT operation rotates row values into columns, turning distinct values of one column into separate output columns and aggregating a measure within each. Some databases (SQL Server, Oracle) provide a dedicated `PIVOT` keyword. When an engine lacks it (PostgreSQL, MySQL, most portable SQL), you reproduce the exact same result with conditional aggregation: a `GROUP BY` combined with one `SUM(CASE WHEN category = 'X' THEN value END)` expression per target column.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the finance team at National Bank of India has a long list of transactions, one row per transaction, each tagged with a channel like ATM, UPI, or NetBanking. A PIVOT turns that tall list into a wide table where ATM, UPI, and NetBanking each become their own column, and each cell holds the total for that channel. It is like taking a vertical ledger and laying it out as a cross-tab spreadsheet.
s1_definition.oneliner: PIVOT turns rows into columns, and `SUM(CASE WHEN ... END)` with GROUP BY does the same thing portably on any database.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A PIVOT operation rotates row values into columns, turning distinct values of one column into separate output columns and aggregating a measure within each. Some databases (SQL Server, Oracle) provide a dedicated `PIVOT` keyword. When an engine lacks it (PostgreSQL, MySQL, most portable SQL), you reproduce the exact same result with conditional aggregation: a `GROUP BY` combined with one `SUM(CASE WHEN category = 'X' THEN value END)` expression per target column.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the finance team at National Bank of India has a long list of transactions, one row per transaction, each tagged with a channel like ATM, UPI, or NetBanking. A PIVOT turns that tall list into a wide table where ATM, UPI, and NetBanking each become their own column, and each cell holds the total for that channel. It is like taking a vertical ledger and laying it out as a cross-tab spreadsheet.

**One line to remember:** PIVOT turns rows into columns, and `SUM(CASE WHEN ... END)` with GROUP BY does the same thing portably on any database.

sections.s2_technical:
A pivot has three ingredients: the grouping column that stays as rows (for example `department`), the pivoting column whose distinct values become new columns (for example `job_title`), and the measure that is aggregated inside each cell (for example `AVG(salary)`). In SQL Server you write it with the `PIVOT` operator and list the target column values explicitly.

The portable technique uses conditional aggregation. You `GROUP BY` the row dimension, and for each value you want as a column you write an aggregate over a `CASE` expression. For example, `SUM(CASE WHEN channel = 'ATM' THEN amount ELSE 0 END) AS atm_total`. The `CASE` returns the amount only for matching rows and zero (or NULL) otherwise, so summing it gives the per-channel total. Using `AVG` instead of `SUM`, and omitting the `ELSE 0` so non-matching rows become NULL (which `AVG` ignores), reproduces an average pivot exactly. For counts you write `COUNT(CASE WHEN channel = 'ATM' THEN 1 END)` — NULL is not counted, so this counts only matching rows.

The portable form has real advantages. It works on every engine, it lets you mix several measures in one query (you can emit both a sum column and a count column per channel), and it is just standard SQL so it is easy to read and test. Its one limitation is that the set of columns is fixed at query-write time: if a new channel appears you must add a new `CASE`. A true `PIVOT` keyword has the same limitation unless you build dynamic SQL. In banking reporting the conditional-aggregation form is almost always preferred because dashboards run against different engines and the column set is known and stable.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India operations dashboard needs a table where each row is a branch region and each column is a payment channel (ATM, UPI, NetBanking), with the total transaction amount in each cell. The raw data is one row per transaction, tall and thin. The dashboard needs it wide. This is exactly a pivot.

Problem 2 — The bank's production databases are a mix: the core ledger runs on PostgreSQL (no `PIVOT` keyword) while an older analytics store ran on SQL Server. The reporting query must work on both, so it cannot use the vendor-specific `PIVOT` syntax. This is why we need the portable `SUM(CASE WHEN ... END)` technique.

Our mini-project builds a `ChannelPivotService` that takes a flat list of transactions and produces a pivoted result: one row per region, with per-channel totals as separate fields. It mirrors exactly what `GROUP BY region` with one `SUM(CASE WHEN channel = ...)` per channel produces in SQL. The code includes a `Transaction` model, a `PivotRow` output model, a repository supplying flat data, the service doing the conditional aggregation, and a runnable demo.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: five transactions — North has ATM Rs.40,000, UPI Rs.15,000, NetBanking Rs.20,000; West has UPI Rs.25,000 and ATM Rs.10,000.

Step 1 — The service reads all five flat transaction rows from the repository. Each row carries a region, a channel, and an amount. This is the tall, thin form.

Step 2 — The service iterates. For each row it records the region in an ordered set and routes the amount into the correct per-channel map using a `switch`, which is the in-memory equivalent of the SQL `CASE WHEN channel = 'ATM' THEN amount`. North's ATM map grows to Rs.40,000, North's UPI to Rs.15,000, and so on. West's UPI reaches Rs.25,000 and West's ATM Rs.10,000.

Step 3 — After the single pass, the service builds one `PivotRow` per region. For North it reads ATM Rs.40,000, UPI Rs.15,000, NetBanking Rs.20,000. For West it reads ATM Rs.10,000, UPI Rs.25,000, and NetBanking defaults to zero because West had no NetBanking transaction. This single-pass grouping is exactly what `GROUP BY region` does.

Step 4 — The wide result is returned and logged, one line per region with three channel columns.

Final output:

```text
2026-10-25 14:46:13 [INFO] === Channel pivot by region (portable conditional aggregation) ===
2026-10-25 14:46:13 [INFO] region=North  ATM=Rs.40000  UPI=Rs.15000  NET=Rs.20000
2026-10-25 14:46:13 [INFO] region=West   ATM=Rs.10000  UPI=Rs.25000  NET=Rs.0
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
A PIVOT operation rotates row values into columns. You pick a dimension that stays as rows, a column whose distinct values each become a new output column, and a measure that is aggregated inside every cell. For example, turning a tall transactions list into a wide table where each payment channel such as ATM, UPI, and NetBanking becomes its own column with the total amount per region in each cell. Some databases such as SQL Server and Oracle provide a dedicated `PIVOT` keyword to express this directly.

When the engine has no `PIVOT` keyword, which is the case for PostgreSQL and MySQL, you reproduce the identical result with conditional aggregation. You group by the row dimension and, for each value you want as a column, you write an aggregate over a `CASE` expression — for instance `SUM(CASE WHEN channel = 'ATM' THEN amount ELSE 0 END)` as the ATM column. The `CASE` yields the amount only for matching rows and zero or NULL otherwise, so the aggregate produces the per-column total. Switching `SUM` to `AVG` and letting non-matching rows become NULL reproduces an average pivot, and `COUNT(CASE WHEN ... THEN 1 END)` reproduces a count pivot because NULL is not counted.

At the National Bank of India our dashboards run against a mix of database engines, so we deliberately avoid the vendor-specific `PIVOT` syntax and always use the portable conditional-aggregation form. It works everywhere, it reads as plain standard SQL, and it lets us emit several measures in one grouped pass, for example both a total and a transaction count per channel side by side. The one trade-off is that the column set is fixed when the query is written, so adding a new channel means adding a new `CASE` expression, but since our channel list is stable and known, that trade-off costs nothing in practice. The line I always state is that PIVOT turns rows into columns, and `SUM(CASE WHEN ... END)` with a GROUP BY does the same thing portably on any database.

keyPoints: GROUP BY: group rows by column values
Aggregate functions: COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX
HAVING: filter groups (vs WHERE which filters rows)
GROUP BY + HAVING vs WHERE: WHERE runs first, HAVING runs after grouping
